sources.citation: Holton, Gary & Laura C. Robinson. 2017. The internal history of the Alor-Pantar language family. In Marian Klamer (ed.), The Alor-Pantar languages: history and typology, 2nd ed., 49-90. Berlin: Language Science Press.
sources.note: Family-level transcription note only, p. 55 (PDF p. 69): 'In most of the modern languages stress is on the penultimate syllable; however, stress may also be attracted to heavy syllables, as in Teiwa jiˈvar "dog". In addition, stress may be phonemically contrastive in some languages, as in Western Pantar baˈwa "conch shell" vs. ˈbawa "drum".' Adang is one of the twelve sampled languages but is not singled out; no Adang stress statement anywhere in the volume (grep of full text). Klamer's ch. 1 typological overview has no stress remark.

sources.citation: Stokhof, W. A. L. 1975. Preliminary notes on the Alor and Pantar languages (East Indonesia). Pacific Linguistics B-43. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: §1.1 (pp. 1-2) defines a prominence mark (') for 'the relative prominence of that vowel as compared to one or more other vowels within the same sound unit', with two peaks (' and ") in longer words; wordlists 17-19 are Kabola (Pitumbang, Aimoli, Hamap), i.e. the Adang-Kabola cluster, with prominence marked per item. No rule statement for any language; scanned text.
